analysis.one_liner: Protects all roadless areas of Alaska's Tongass National Forest from logging, mining, and road-building.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced with no cosponsors in late November 2002, it was sent to a House committee the same day and died there when the Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have permanently protected every roadless area in Alaska's Tongass National Forest — the largest temperate rain forest in the United States — by barring logging, mining, road construction, and motorized vehicles there, and would have created a 46,100-acre wilderness area on Duke Island. It also let the Forest Service buy private land inside the forest from willing sellers, or take an especially important parcel through eminent domain with full market-value compensation. The bill was introduced on November 22, 2002, with no cosponsors, referred to the House Resources Committee and its forests subcommittee the same day, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses or values public lands: hunters, anglers, subsistence users, tourists, and residents of Southeast Alaska who rely on intact old-growth forest for salmon habitat, wildlife like bears, wolves, and bald eagles, and the region's growing tourism economy. The bill's findings also argued that taxpayers benefit because the Forest Service has historically spent public money building logging roads into the Tongass for a small number of timber operators, so ending roadless-area logging would end that subsidy. Future generations get an intact rain forest preserved in perpetuity.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Public-lands users and Southeast Alaska residents

how_it_helps.text: Designates all Tongass roadless areas as the Tongass Rainforest Nature Preserve, where logging, mining, road-building, structures, and motorized equipment are prohibited in perpetuity. [S2] [S3]

Creates the Duke Island Trumpeter Swan Wilderness Area of about 46,100 acres as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, protecting habitat for trumpeter swans, goshawks, Peregrine falcons, black bears, and Steller sea lions. [S2] [S3]

The bill's findings state that federal policies subsidize destruction of the Tongass and undermine U.S. credibility in urging other countries to protect tropical rain forests — meaning the bill aimed to stop taxpayer-funded logging-road subsidies. [S3]

Allows the Secretary of Agriculture to acquire private inholdings from willing sellers, and rare biologically or scenically important inholdings through eminent domain at full fair market value, closing gaps in protection while paying owners fairly. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Timber companies and their contractors, who would lose access to old-growth stands in roadless areas, and mining companies seeking claims in the protected lands. Taxpayers would fund any inholding purchases. Some Southeast Alaska logging-dependent communities and workers would bear the economic cost of a larger protected area, though the bill did not address their transition.

drawbacks.text: The bill would eliminate timber jobs and economic activity in Southeast Alaska communities that depend on Tongass logging, without offering any transition assistance for affected workers or towns. [S3]

Its language is broad: it bans 'any activity that disturbs native animal and plant species or their habitats' in a forest that already has roads, settlements, and long-standing uses nearby, which could create practical conflicts for neighboring landowners and established access. The eminent domain provision, though compensated at full market value, would still let the government force sales of private land inside the forest. [S2] [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is genuine: permanent protection of the nation's largest temperate rain forest against continued old-growth timber and mineral extraction. The bill protected the forest but provided nothing for workers or communities who would lose timber income, and its sweeping habitat-protection language could have created administrative conflicts. Even so, the benefits — permanent salmon and wildlife habitat, preserved public lands, and an end to subsidized logging-road construction — would accrue broadly to the public and would be permanent.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with zero cosponsors on the last working stretch of the Congress, referred to the Resources Committee and its forests subcommittee the same day, and simply expired there with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Israel introduced the Tongass Rain Forest Protection Act in the House on November 22, 2002. [S1] [S5]
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor. [S4]
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources and directly to its Subcommittee on Forests and Forest Health on the day of introduction. [S5]
The subcommittee and full committee took no further action, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber and mining industries and the beneficiaries of continued Tongass roadless-area logging — including operators who rely on Forest Service-funded roads — were better off because the bill died, since the old-growth stands it would have closed remained available. Public-lands advocates lost the chance for statutory protection, though roadless-area policy remained contested administratively.

for.name: Rep. Steve Israel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 22, 2002 and referred it to the House Resources Committee; no other member joined as a cosponsor. [S1] [S4] [S5]

against.name: House Committee on Resources leadership
against.role: Chairman of the committee that controlled the bill's fate
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended. [S5]

against.name: Alaska congressional delegation
against.role: Alaska's senators and representatives, who historically opposed Tongass wilderness designations
against.what_they_did: Defended continued logging and development access in the Tongass; no Tongass wilderness bill advanced in this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. The bill had one Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, so no party position was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have permanently closed Tongass roadless old-growth to logging, ending the industry's access to the largest temperate rain forest in the U.S. — access that the bill's findings say has been supported by federal logging-road subsidies paid by taxpayers. [S3]
Mining and mineral extraction would be prohibited throughout the designated preserve. [S2]
Road construction in the preserve is banned, eliminating a source of Forest Service-funded work. [S3]
Preserving intact old-growth forest protects salmon streams and wildlife habitat that the region's recreation, tourism, and fishing economies depend on.
